moduleMetadata.title: Mobile & Remote Work Security
moduleMetadata.description: Learn to secure your devices and maintain cybersecurity best practices while working from home or in public spaces.
moduleMetadata.whyThisMatters: Cybersecurity does not stop when you leave the office. Today, people access organizational systems from smartphones, tablets, laptops, home networks, and public Wi-Fi. Working outside a traditional office can create additional risks because devices may be lost, stolen, connected to unfamiliar networks, or used around other people.
moduleMetadata.learningOutcome: Users should understand how to maintain cybersecurity while using mobile devices or working remotely.

learningObjectives: Apply mobile device security features like screen locking and encryption.
Evaluate application permissions and update software regularly.
Recognize the risks of public Wi-Fi and use secure access methods.
Implement physical device protection in public or home settings.
Understand the reporting process for lost or stolen devices.

sections.title: Mobile Device Security
sections.content: Your phone is a powerful computer that contains vast amounts of personal and work data.

subsections.title: Screen Locking
subsections.content: Always use a PIN, password, or biometric lock. A device without a lock screen is an open door to your data.

subsections.title: Application Permissions
subsections.content: Be wary of apps that ask for more access than they need (e.g., a calculator asking for your location and contacts).

sections.title: Public Wi-Fi Awareness
sections.content: Public Wi-Fi (in cafes, hotels, or airports) is often unencrypted and can be monitored by attackers.
tips: Avoid accessing sensitive accounts (banking, work) on public Wi-Fi.
Use a Virtual Private Network (VPN) to encrypt your traffic.

sections.title: Remote Work Security
sections.content: Working from home requires the same level of caution as the office.
bulletPoints: Secure your home Wi-Fi with a strong password.
Keep work devices separate from personal use when possible.
Don't let family members or guests use your work laptop.

sections.title: Physical Security and Shoulder Surfing
sections.content: Physical threats are more common when working remotely.

subsections.title: Shoulder Surfing
subsections.content: People nearby can see your screen or watch you type passwords. Use privacy screens in public.

subsections.title: Device Theft
subsections.content: Never leave your laptop or phone unattended in a public space, even for a minute.

interactiveExercises.title: H.O.M.E. and D.E.V.I.C.E. Routine
interactiveExercises.instruction: Map your daily remote work routine to identify potential security gaps.

interactiveExercises.title: Permission Evaluation
interactiveExercises.question: A simple 'Flashlight App' asks for the following permissions. Which one is a red flag?
interactiveExercises.explanation: A flashlight app has no legitimate reason to access your personal contacts or call logs.

scenarios.title: Hotel Guest Wi-Fi
scenarios.content: You are at a hotel and see two networks: 'Hotel_Guest_WiFi' and 'Hotel_Free_HighSpeed_WiFi' (no password).
scenarios.action: Use the official network with a password and your VPN. The free, open network might be a 'Twin' set up by an attacker.

choices.text: Join the open "Hotel_Free_HighSpeed_WiFi" — it is faster and has no password hassle
choices.consequence: An open network with a friendly name is the classic "evil twin" setup. All traffic you send is visible to whoever is running it, including your logins.

choices.text: Join the official password-protected network and use a VPN for sensitive traffic
choices.consequence: The password-protected network is the one the hotel actually operates. Adding a VPN on top encrypts your traffic end-to-end, even if the hotel network itself is later compromised.

choices.text: Turn off Wi-Fi and use your phone's mobile data only
choices.consequence: Mobile data is generally safer than open Wi-Fi, but you lose the ability to use the hotel network for your laptop at all — a reasonable fallback, but unnecessary when a secured network exists.

choices.text: Ask the front desk which network is real, then connect to whichever they name without further checks
choices.consequence: Front-desk staff can be mistaken, and an attacker could have given them the wrong name too. Pair the staff answer with the password-protected network and a VPN for real confidence.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Join the official password-protected network and use a VPN for sensitive traffic

scenarios.title: The Cafe Coffee Break
scenarios.content: You are working in a crowded cafe. You need to step away for 60 seconds to grab your coffee from the counter.
scenarios.action: Lock your screen and take your device with you, or at least ensure it is physically secured and locked.
scenarios.lesson: A minute is all it takes for someone to steal a device or insert a malicious USB.

choices.text: Leave the laptop open and unlocked — you will only be gone a minute
choices.consequence: A minute is enough for a passerby to plug in a malicious USB, copy open files, or walk away with the device. Physical access beats most software defenses.

choices.text: Lock the screen (Win+L / Cmd+Ctrl+Q) and take the device with you
choices.consequence: The device is both physically and logically protected while you step away. Even if someone grabs it, they still face the screen lock.

choices.text: Close the lid but leave it unlocked
choices.consequence: Closing the lid may not lock the session depending on power settings. The device is still easy to grab and open without a password.

choices.text: Ask a stranger at the next table to watch it
choices.consequence: You just asked an unknown person to be responsible for your work device. They have no obligation to protect it and may themselves be a threat.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Lock the screen (Win+L / Cmd+Ctrl+Q) and take the device with you

scenarios.title: Shoulder Surfing in the Park
scenarios.content: You are reviewing a confidential report on a bench. You notice someone sitting close behind you who seems to be looking at your screen.
scenarios.action: Adjust your position, use a privacy filter, or stop working on sensitive data until you are in a private area.
scenarios.lesson: Be aware of your physical surroundings when accessing sensitive data.

choices.text: Keep working — they are probably just looking at the scenery
choices.consequence: Shoulder surfing is a real, low-tech attack. A few seconds of visibility on a password, email subject line, or confidential report is enough to leak it.

choices.text: Adjust your position, tilt the screen, or move to a more private area before continuing
choices.consequence: You remove the line of sight without drawing attention. Confidential work stays confidential and you can continue safely.

choices.text: Confront the person and ask them to move
choices.consequence: Confrontation can escalate and rarely proves intent. They can simply move a few feet and continue watching from a different angle.

choices.text: Take a photo of the person as evidence
choices.consequence: Photographing a stranger can be unlawful depending on jurisdiction and may escalate a situation that is easier to solve by simply moving.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Adjust your position, tilt the screen, or move to a more private area before continuing

scenarios.title: The Missing Laptop
scenarios.content: You realize your corporate laptop was stolen from your car trunk.
scenarios.action: Report it to IT and the police immediately. Speed is critical for remote wiping and disabling access.
scenarios.lesson: Immediate reporting minimizes the window for data exploitation.

choices.text: Wait a day to see if it turns up — it might just be misplaced
choices.consequence: Every hour the device is out of your control is an hour an attacker has to extract data, clone the disk, or use cached sessions to access your accounts.

choices.text: Report it to IT and local law enforcement immediately so remote wipe and account revocation can start
choices.consequence: Fast reporting lets IT issue a remote wipe, revoke tokens, and reset passwords tied to the device. A police report is often required for insurance and compliance.

choices.text: Try to track it yourself using a consumer "find my device" service
choices.consequence: Consumer tracking may work, but it does not trigger the remote wipe or token revocation that actually protects the data on the device.

choices.text: Change your own passwords from your phone and hope for the best
choices.consequence: Changing passwords is useful but incomplete. Sessions, tokens, and cached credentials on the stolen device still work until IT revokes them.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Report it to IT and local law enforcement immediately so remote wipe and account revocation can start

quiz.question: What is the most basic security measure for a mobile device?
options: A screen lock (PIN, Password, or Biometric).
quiz.correctAnswer: A screen lock (PIN, Password, or Biometric).
quiz.explanation: Screen locks prevent immediate access to your data if the device is lost or stolen.

quiz.question: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) is used to:
options: Encrypt your data and create a secure connection over the internet.
quiz.correctAnswer: Encrypt your data and create a secure connection over the internet.
quiz.explanation: VPNs are essential for protecting data on untrusted networks like public Wi-Fi.

quiz.question: What is 'Shoulder Surfing'?
options: Looking over someone's shoulder to see their screen or keystrokes.
Surfing the web while standing up.
quiz.correctAnswer: Looking over someone's shoulder to see their screen or keystrokes.
quiz.explanation: It's a low-tech way to steal passwords or sensitive information.

quiz.question: Is it safe to let a friend use your work laptop to check their email?
options: No, work devices should only be used by authorized personnel.
Only if they use a guest account.
Yes, as long as you are watching.
quiz.correctAnswer: No, work devices should only be used by authorized personnel.
quiz.explanation: Work devices contain sensitive data and access that should not be shared.

quiz.question: What should you do before installing a new app on your phone?
options: Check its reviews and the permissions it requests.
quiz.correctAnswer: Check its reviews and the permissions it requests.
quiz.explanation: Reviewing permissions helps you identify potential malware or privacy risks.

quiz.question: Why should you disable 'Auto-Join' for Wi-Fi?
options: It prevents your device from connecting to a malicious network with a familiar name.
It makes your phone look cooler.
It stops you from using the internet.
quiz.correctAnswer: It prevents your device from connecting to a malicious network with a familiar name.
quiz.explanation: Attackers can create faked networks that match common names (like 'Starbucks_WiFi') to trick devices.

quiz.question: If you lose your work phone, when should you report it?
options: After you've looked for it for a few days.
Next time you are in the office.
Only if you think someone stole it.
quiz.explanation: Prompt reporting allows the organization to secure the account and wipe the device.

quiz.question: Encryption on a mobile device:
options: Scrambles the data so it cannot be read without the correct key.
quiz.correctAnswer: Scrambles the data so it cannot be read without the correct key.
quiz.explanation: Encryption is a vital layer of protection for stored data.

keyTakeaways: Secure your devices with strong locks and encryption.
Be skeptical of public Wi-Fi; use a VPN.
Protect your device physically and avoid shoulder surfing.
Report lost or stolen work devices immediately.
reflectApply: Open your phone settings. Do you have a screen lock enabled? Is your data encrypted?
Review your app list. Are there any apps you haven't used in months that still have access to your location or contacts?
